sentences: In the dim light sits a bodhisattva with a soft golden glow.
One leg rests across the other knee, and the fingertips barely touch the cheek, lost in thought.
Begin by taking in the whole figure, slowly.
In Korean the pose is called bangasayu: half-cross-legged, contemplating.
Bodhisattvas in this pose are usually identified as Maitreya, the Buddha of the future.
This one is thought to date from the early 7th century and stands 93.
5 centimetres high.
Look first at the crown.
It is a very simple one, made of three low peaks.
Unlike other pensive figures with ornate headdresses, this one strips decoration away.
Now come down to the face.
The eyes are lowered and half closed, and a faint smile rests at the corners of the mouth.
It suggests not anguish but the calm that comes just before enlightenment.
The right fingertips hover, just grazing the cheek.
Each finger bends a little differently, as if a thought were stirring at that very moment.
Try looking at these fingertips from a slightly different angle.
The upper body is bare except for a single necklace.
The contour from shoulders to waist is pared down, with nothing extra.
That is why the body looks slender and sturdy at the same time.
The right foot rests on the left knee, and the left hand lightly holds the ankle.
Look at the foot, and you will see the toes turned slightly upward.
A small tension hides inside this stillness.
In contrast with the plain upper body, the skirt draped over the seat ripples down like water.
Layer upon layer of folds gives rhythm to a still figure.
Calm above, flowing like water below.
The figure was cast in bronze and then gilded, which is what we call gilt bronze.
Casting it this thin at this size, in such balance, was the highest technical achievement of its time.
The left foot, set on a lotus, carries it all.
At Kōryū-ji temple in Kyoto, Japan, there is a wooden pensive figure with almost the same pose and proportions.
Scholars still debate how the two are related, and whether this bronze was made in Silla or in Baekje.
In 2021 the National Museum of Korea opened the Room of Quiet Contemplation for just two pensive bodhisattvas.
Its floor and walls tilt almost imperceptibly, and the walls are finished by hand in red clay.
Today the two sit there side by side.
Finally, step back and look at the smile once more.
What might this pensive thought, held for nearly fourteen hundred years, have been?
And what are you thinking about today?
